title: Black Friday Shoppers Watch Budgets. Storms Knock Out Power. Stock Futures Jump.
subject: Black Friday Shoppers Watch Budgets. Storms Knock Out Power. Stock Futures Jump.
preview_text: Careful Black Friday shoppers, storm outages, a futures rally and New Zealand's coalition math.
description: Black Friday shoppers mix gifts with essentials. Storms left hundreds of thousands without power, and stock futures climbed before a short session.
contents_extra: Why the Gulf conflict is flaring again, trivia and your poll

stories.title: Black Friday Shoppers Mix Gifts With Everyday Essentials

photo.alt: Shoppers in a busy mall; file photo.

paragraphs: Black Friday remains the biggest day of the year for foot traffic at physical stores, AP reports, citing Sensormatic Solutions. Consumers spent $82.5 billion online from Nov. 1 to Nov. 22, according to Adobe. Analysts said shoppers are also stocking up on discounted household basics.

The National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday sales rising 4.2% to just above $1 trillion, Reuters reports via NBC News. Much of the gain reflects 3.8% inflation. Chicago shoppers told CBS they are keeping budgets in mind amid affordability concerns.

stories.title: Storms Leave Hundreds of Thousands Without Power After Thanksgiving

photo.alt: Lightning near a power tower; file photo.

paragraphs: Almost 700,000 customers were still without power early Friday, according to PowerOutage.us, NBC News reports. Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland were hardest hit. That was down from a peak of about 940,000 on Thanksgiving.

NBC News reports 462 flights were canceled Thursday, citing FlightAware. Heavy storms disrupted travel across the country on the holiday, AP reports via Al Jazeera. Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain, NBC News reports, citing the National Weather Service.

stories.title: Stock Futures Jump Ahead of a Shortened Friday Session

photo.alt: Market quotes on screens; file photo.

paragraphs: S&P 500 futures were up nearly 2% and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 2.8% early Friday, CNBC reported as of 4:12 a.m. ET. Dow futures were up 655 points. The stock market is scheduled to close at 1 p.m. ET Friday.

CNBC said the S&P 500 is up almost 4% week to date. AI-related stocks gave back some gains after Monday. A study spanning 170 years put the probability of an AI-driven bubble as high as 97%, CNBC reports. Two other models estimated about 40%.

stories.title: New Zealand's Ruling Coalition Falls One Seat Short of a Majority
paragraphs: Official results Friday showed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon fell just short of a parliamentary majority, Reuters reports. His coalition holds 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament. Luxon will seek support from the centrist Opportunity Party, which won seven seats.

Analysts told Reuters a fresh election was unlikely, but talks could run into next year. "Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart," Luxon said. The results offer no clear path to forming a government, Al Jazeera reports.

deep_dive.title: Why the Gulf Conflict Is Flaring Again

photo.alt: A large cargo ship with tugboats; file photo.

paragraphs: What happened. Two Italians were killed in an alleged attack on Kuwait, Kuwaiti forces said Thursday, CNBC reports. Kuwait's army said falling missile debris after Iranian attacks caused the deaths. Separately, an aerial projectile hit a Saudi refinery in Jazan on Thursday, killing one worker, according to Saudi Arabia's energy ministry.

Why it matters. The Jazan refinery near the Yemeni border can process up to 400,000 barrels of crude a day, Al Jazeera reports. The ministry said the strike caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations. A Saudi-led coalition said Yemen's Houthis attacked it. The group had claimed attacks on Ras Tanura a day earlier.

What each side says. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had no role in the Kuwait incident, CNBC reports. He called it "suspicious" and offered to help investigate. An Israeli military spokesman said Israel was prepared to strike Iran "at any moment," even without U.S. forces. Trump said on PBS that victory was "at hand."

What comes next. Iran's armed forces chief of staff warned the US and Israel against attacking Iran, Al Jazeera reports. Ali Abdollahi said the navy would deliver a firm response to any aggression. Trump said Washington was still giving Iran "every chance to make a deal," CNBC reports. He said he was unsure Tehran would agree.

World view: Zelenskyy warns of a new Russian strike. He said Thursday that Russia is preparing another major attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure; AP reports.
China rehearses landings near Taiwan. Satellite images showed a drill linking civilian vessels into a makeshift floating bridge in Fujian; Reuters reports via NBC News.
Costa Rica bars a UN rapporteur. Authorities cited national security in barring Francesca Albanese, who called her detention a "disgrace"; Al Jazeera reports.
Spain's far right eyes power. Vox has pledged to prioritize Spanish citizens over immigrants if empowered after Sunday's national election; AP reports via NBC News.
Need to know: Iowa blast test results are near. Results from sampling after the Army's lead azide detonation could start coming in Friday, the EPA said; AP reports via NBC News.
Strobe Talbott dies at 80. The former deputy secretary of state under Bill Clinton later headed the Brookings Institution; AP reports via NBC News.
A pregnant inmate escapes in New Mexico. Officials said she took control of a transport SUV after a prenatal appointment in Albuquerque; NBC News reports.
More holiday travelers skip planes. AAA projected 81.5 million Americans traveling at least 50 miles, with more taking buses, trains and cruises; CNBC reports.
Money & markets: China's chip stocks soar. The CSI Semiconductor index climbed 17.6% Friday after policymakers pledged a bigger role for state-backed funds; CNBC reports.
Chinese factory profits jump. Industrial profits rose 20.1% in October from a year earlier, the fastest pace since May; CNBC reports.
Rheinmetall trims its outlook. The German arms maker now expects 2030 sales of 33 billion to 37 billion euros, down from about 45 billion; CNBC reports.
Argentina limits its central bank. Lawmakers gave final approval to a bill barring the bank from printing money for government spending; Al Jazeera reports.
Future frontiers: A Russian cargo ship reaches the station. Progress 97 docked Thursday with about three tons of food, fuel and supplies; NASA said.
Nvidia chip buyers face a China test. Two people told CNBC chip sellers won't supply neoclouds that rent computing capacity to Chinese companies; CNBC reports.
SAP weighs big AI-era job cuts. The software giant is weighing at least 10,000 job cuts, citing people familiar with the matter; Bloomberg reported, via CNBC.
SpaceX shares climb premarket. Elon Musk said he would donate an additional SpaceX share to every child in America each year; CNBC reports.
The score: Buffalo beats Kansas City at the gun. Tyler Bass hit a 57-yard field goal as time expired for a 13-10 Bills win; ESPN reports.
Joe Milton powers an Eagles comeback. He accounted for four touchdowns in a 39-38 win over the Cowboys on Thursday; ESPN reports.
Chicago stuns Detroit. Caleb Williams found Rome Odunze with nine seconds left as the Bears won 39-35; ESPN reports.
Tomlin weighs in on Rodgers. Mike Tomlin called the Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy situation "a dumpster fire"; ESPN reports.
Life & culture: Sportswear brands pile into F1. Sportswear sponsorship spending in Formula 1 has surged 75% over two years, according to Ampere Analysis; CNBC reports.
Crunchy food is having a moment. Texture-maxxing is a social media trend as consumers seek a more sensory food experience; CNBC reports.
Microdrama apps chase profits. The US microdrama industry is projected to generate $1.5 billion in revenue in 2026; CNBC reports.
GTA VI sets a sales record. The game had a $3.79 billion opening, though some experts doubt it will revive the industry; NBC News reports.

trivia.question: How many customers were still without power early Friday after the Thanksgiving storms?
trivia.explanation: B. Almost 700,000. Almost 700,000 customers were still without power early Friday, NBC News reports, citing PowerOutage.us.
